edgeReasons.reason: the engine runs an integration's block, and the connection state, the connection values and the context an integration receives are resolved in exactly one place (apps/worker/src/services/integrations). The exception names services/integrations/runtime.ts, which re-exports those reads and none of the write surface: a run may use a connection and may never change one. A second resolution in the engine is how a palette and a run come to disagree about the same deployment.

the registry holds the integrations and the SDK and nothing else. It is generated by pnpm run gen:integrations, so an edge out of it is a generator change, not an edit: whatever it needs from core belongs in the hand-written entry that re-exports it, or in the caller.

the host UI is what the dashboard lends an integration, so it holds primitives and the page contract and nothing else. It may read the SDK's manifest types, because the pages it types are the pages a manifest declares. It may not read the dashboard: a package that imported an app would invert the dependency and put a screen's internals into a contract with third-party code.

an integration imports @integrations/sdk, @integrations/host-ui and its provider's own packages, and nothing else in this repository. What it needs from core reaches it through the context the SDK describes and the primitives the host UI lends.

core may not import an integration. Ask the generated registry instead: @integrations/registry for the manifests (plain data, safe in a browser and in the Workflow DevKit flow bundle) and @integrations/registry/worker for the runtimes (server only). pnpm run gen:integrations writes both.

forbiddenImports.reason: the dashboard runs in a browser and the worker registry imports every integration's server code, provider SDKs and Node modules included. Read what the screen needs from @integrations/registry, which is manifest data.

the registry's root entry is read in a browser and inside the Workflow DevKit flow bundle, where a Node module fails the Vercel build and nothing local. Worker entries belong in @integrations/registry/worker.

the dashboard registry holds React components. The worker is a Nitro bundle with no React in it, and the Workflow DevKit traces its imports, so reaching this file breaks the Vercel build and nothing local. The worker asks @integrations/registry, which is manifest data.
the registry's other entries are read where there is no React: the worker, and the Workflow DevKit flow bundle. Keeping the dashboard entry off them is what lets one package serve three bundles.

an integration's dashboard entry is compiled into the cockpit's bundle. Its worker entry is server code with provider SDKs and Node modules in it, so importing one from the other puts them in a browser. Share plain data through a third file in the package.

forbiddenSpecifiers.reason: `@/` is the dashboard's own alias. An integration reaching through it pins itself to a screen's internals, which change whenever a screen needs them to. Import @integrations/host-ui, which is the UI the host lends and is a contract that only grows.

an integration's dashboard entry is a Server Component in our process, so these are the doors that let one stop being a page and start being part of the cockpit: next/headers reaches our cookies, next/navigation moves the person, node: reaches the filesystem, and server-only is how a module says it is ours. Integration code is trusted code we review, and this rule is what keeps a page from coupling itself to our runtime by accident. A page renders what its own package knows; if it needs more, that is a contract change, not an import.
